euv-fab-intensity.title: EUV tools per fab & leading-edge capex intensity (per 10kwpm)
euv-fab-intensity.definition: Conversion constants for capex<->wafers<->EUV-unit sizing: EUV tools required per kwpm of leading-edge/DRAM capacity, and $ capex per 10kwpm. ALWAYS state node + whether the EUV throughput is nameplate or real-world derated.
euv-fab-intensity.canonical: N2 logic (Bristlemoon, Jun-2026): ~11 EUV tools per 25kwpm fab and ~US$4.7B TOTAL fab capex per 10kwpm, built on real EUV throughput ~1/3 of nameplate (NXE:3800E 220->165 wph @40mJ dose x 45% uptime -> 34% OEE -> 2,430 wpm/tool) and 25kwpm as the modern module size (no longer ~40kwpm); capex stack: tool $240M -> EUV 80% of litho -> litho 40% of WFE -> WFE 70% of fab total. Cross-check (former Samsung foundry EVP, Jun-2026): ~10-12 EUV machines per fab, each ~$400M incl. 5-10yr maintenance, ~100 wafers/hr; litho ~35-40% of advanced-node (<=4/3/2nm) equipment capex; ~$20B fab / ~$14B equipment. DRAM basis differs: ~57 EUV tools for HBM by 2028E on rising EUV layers/wafer (3->6, '25-'28).
euv-fab-intensity.scope_note: Bristlemoon's $4.7B/10kwpm is TOTAL fab capex (litho+WFE+shell), NOT WFE-only or EUV-only. Real vs nameplate EUV throughput differ ~3x — never size tools off nameplate. Logic (22 EUV layers @ N2) vs DRAM (3-6 EUV layers/wafer) intensities are different bases.

rev-per-gw.title: AI compute revenue / rental rate per GW
rev-per-gw.definition: Annualized $ revenue (or rental rate) per GW of AI compute capacity — state chip type (ASIC vs merchant GPU) and whether it is a rental rate or realized revenue. Distinct from facility BUILD cost per GW.
rev-per-gw.canonical: Rental/revenue per GW of compute: Trainium <$10B/GW (Anthropic/OpenAI); merchant GPU ~$12-13B/GW (neocloud & AWS, pre-2H26 shortage); premium GPU ~$25B/GW (~$25M/MW/yr, SpaceX–Google deal). MS pegs 1P merchant TPU at ~$20B rev/GW (20% GM base). Colocation POWER-ONLY rent: ~$60/kW-month historically -> ~$120-160 typical now, up to ~$200 (weak-credit tenant + good DC), as low as ~$80-100 (India / mid DC / poor grid). Rev/GW is a data-center-QUALITY metric: credit, utilization, networking and speed-to-market drive a ~2x spread — a top-operator GW ≈ 2x a generic GW. NEW (08-28): lab INFERENCE MONETISATION ~$60-100bn/GW/yr (Baker/a16z) — a distinct, much larger basis than the rental rates; implies ~1yr REVENUE payback on a ~$50bn/GW build. Neocloud payback marked at ~9-10 months (50-60% collected upfront).
rev-per-gw.scope_note: THREE distinct bases — never mix: (a) compute rev/rental $/GW (ASIC vs GPU, the monetization/quality metric); (b) colocation $/kW-month = power+shell only, NOT compute; (c) facility BUILD cost ~$30-40B/GW (ASIC) vs ~$50B/GW (NVDA-GPU infra) — see custom-asic-tpu. A $/kW-month figure ×12×1e6 ≈ $/GW-year only for the power-shell layer, not the compute. ⚠️ FOURTH BASIS ADDED 2026-08-28 — LAB MONETISATION per GW (~$60-100bn/GW/yr) is what the LAB EARNS on a GW, and is 3-10x the RENTAL rates above (~$10-25bn/GW/yr) and ~1-2x the ~$50bn/GW BUILD cost. Never compare it to a rental rate: renting a GW at ~$12-13bn and monetising at ~$60-100bn implies a 5-8x gross spread, which is either (a) list/aspirational rather than realised, (b) not utilisation-matched, or (c) evidence the rental marks are stale (they are flagged pre-2H26-shortage). UNRECONCILED — treat the spread as an open question, not a margin. 🔴 FIFTH AND SIXTH BASES ADDED 2026-09-02 (Broadcom Q3 FY26 call, which produced THREE different per-GW numbers in one hour): (e) VENDOR SILICON CONTENT per GW = $20-30bn (AVGO's XPU + networking silicon into a rack someone else integrates) — this is NOT the same quantity as NVDA's $25-40bn+/GW, which is FULL-RACK REFERENCE-DESIGN revenue and only applies if the customer buys the whole design; and (f) VENDOR REVENUE per DEMAND-GW = $11-12bn (AVGO's guide divided by AVGO's own GW ladder). (e) and (f) differ by ~2x and BOTH come from the same company on the same call — the reconciliation is that demand GW ≠ shipped GW, so ~$345bn of FY27-28 revenue at $20-30bn/GW implies only ~12-17GW ships against ~30GW of demand. ⚠️ SIX bases now circulate: rental $/GW · colo $/kW-month · build cost $/GW · lab monetisation $/GW · vendor silicon content $/GW · vendor revenue per demand-GW. Never net or chain them.

rev-per-gw.debate: Rev/GW is emerging as a data-center-quality metric: ASIC (<$10B) < merchant GPU ($12-13B) < premium operator ($25B). The spread reflects credit quality, utilization, networking and speed-to-market — not just chip type. Watch whether the 2H26 GPU shortage pushes realized GPU rev/GW above the $12-13B pre-shortage mark. OPEN (08-28): the ~5-8x gap between what a lab is said to monetise per GW ($60-100bn) and what a GW rents for ($12-13bn merchant GPU) is unreconciled and is the single highest-value thing to verify in this metric — it is either the strongest ROI evidence in the corpus or a basis error. 🔴 MATERIAL UPDATE 2026-09-02 — THE HIGHEST-VALUE OPEN QUESTION IN THIS METRIC JUST GOT AN INDEPENDENT MARK, AND IT IS 2-3x LOWER. Hock Tan put LAB revenue at ~$30bn/GW/yr — the SAME quantity Gavin Baker put at $60-100bn/GW on 08-28. Broadcom is a direct supplier with contractual visibility into these labs' deployment schedules and is using the figure to underwrite its OWN credit exposure, which argues for taking it seriously and probably argues it is conservative-to-realistic rather than aspirational. That narrows the unreconciled spread against the $12-13bn merchant-GPU rental mark from ~5-8x to ~2.3-2.5x — a plausible gross spread rather than a suspected basis error. ➤ REVISED READ: the Baker $60-100bn figure now looks like the outlier and should be treated as list/aspirational or not utilisation-matched, not as the canonical lab-monetisation rate. Keep both; lead with the $30bn mark.

wafers-per-gw.title: Wafers per GW of AI compute — node split (N3 / N5 / DRAM)
wafers-per-gw.definition: 300mm wafer starts needed to BUILD 1 GW of AI compute, split by node/type. A one-time wafer BILL per GW, not a standing monthly capacity — never mix with the WSPM cards. Every figure must carry (a) its rack denominator (racks/GW and the kW/rack behind it), (b) its GW basis (compute-TDP / IT-load vs facility), and (c) whether it is logic-only (foundry) or all-wafer (logic + DRAM + NAND).
wafers-per-gw.canonical: Rack denominator for VR200 is FIRM at ~4,440-4,545 racks/GW on an IT-load/compute-TDP basis — TrendForce ~225kW/rack (2026-06-28) and Bernstein 220kW compute-TDP (2026-07-20) agree independently. On that denominator, 1 GW of Vera Rubin ≈ 230-295k total 300mm wafers: DRAM 141-205k (house bottom-up; central ~155-186k) and foundry logic 25-30k (house bottom-up) vs Patel's 61k. The DRAM leg is well-anchored; the LOGIC leg is the live dispute — Patel's 55k N3 + 6k N5 is ~2x a die-area bottom-up of the NVL144 rack BOM and ~2.9x Fubon's Blackwell card (33k TSMC wafers/GW at 7,200 NVL72 racks = 4.6 wafers/rack).
wafers-per-gw.scope_note: THREE traps. (1) Rack denominator: Blackwell GB300 ~150kW => 7,200 racks/GW (Fubon) vs VR200 ~220-225kW => ~4,440-4,545 racks/GW vs Redburn's FACILITY-GW frame (PUE 1.15, 90% to GPU racks, 250kW/rack) => 3,130 racks/GW. Wafers/GW scales inversely with kW/rack. (2) JPM's VR200 'rack design power' of 330-444kW is NAMEPLATE, not draw — do not build a rack count on it. (3) logic-only vs all-wafer: Fubon's 33k is foundry wafers only; Bernstein's 65 wafers/rack and the AlphaSense 350k are all-wafer.

wafers-per-gw.debate: The LOGIC leg. 55k N3 + 6k N5 = 61k foundry wafers/GW ⇒ 13.4 logic wafers/rack, against ~5.5-6.5 from a die-area bottom-up of the NVL144 BOM (144 Rubin dies ~750mm², 65-70 gross/wafer, 50-60% AI-die yield ⇒ ~4.0 wafers; + Vera CPU ~0.5, NVLink-6 switch ~1.0, CX9/BlueField ~1.0) and against Fubon's 4.6 wafers/rack on Blackwell. The DRAM leg pins the denominator at ~4,400-4,545 racks/GW (a facility-GW denominator of 3,130 racks would require ~480GB per HBM wafer = a ~5:1 displacement vs DDR5, worse than MU's own ~4:1 at HBM4E — unlikely, though not impossible), so the gap cannot be explained by the GW basis — it has to be extra silicon (Rubin CPX, standalone Vera CPU racks, LPU racks, Spectrum-6/CX9 CPO) or a much worse yield assumption. Note CPX cannot close it at JPM's assumption of 144 CPX/rack at only 10-15% attach in 2027/28. Unresolved: what Patel's 55k N3 actually covers — the NVL144 compute rack alone or the whole Rubin family — is not stated in the excerpt, and the figures are ~2Q26 vintage.

ai-cyber-net-effect.title: AI × cyber — net additive or destructive to the vendor P&L
ai-cyber-net-effect.definition: The size of the AI-driven incremental cyber opportunity vs the share of today's cyber market at risk of AI-native / frontier-lab disruption.
ai-cyber-net-effect.canonical: ~$220bn incremental cyber opportunity from greater AI threat vs ~10% of the cyber market at risk of disruption → a market ~10% LARGER in the out-years (MS Marshall/Weiss, 'AI-Natives: Challengers, or Creating Challenges, for Cyber', 2026-04-20). Disruption risk is concentrated in the PREVENTATIVE layer (vulnerability mgmt, AppSec testing, posture); control-point and runtime 'require low-latency, deterministic responses' — a claim about today's models.
ai-cyber-net-effect.scope_note: The offset relies on an exhibit whose basis includes '35% of services can be automated with AI' — part of the disruption is assumed INTO services, not into vendor revenue. The stocks traded ~(25%) into the note. Do not net the $220bn against the spend ladder as if it were incremental vendor revenue: it is an opportunity sizing, not a forecast.

ai-vuln-discovery-unit-cost.title: Unit cost of AI vulnerability discovery / remediation — the harness-vs-model economics
ai-vuln-discovery-unit-cost.definition: What a frontier model costs per unit of security work (per token, per critical finding, per remediation) versus the incumbents' harness and versus runtime products' per-transaction cost — THREE different units that must never be compared across.
ai-vuln-discovery-unit-cost.canonical: Frontier: Claude Mythos Preview $25 / $125 per million input/output tokens, 5x Opus 4.6's $5/$25 (WSJ via Stratechery, 2026-04-08). Finding cost: PANW burned '>$1 million worth of tokens' to find >24 critical vulnerabilities in ~3 weeks (~5x its normal tooling) → ~$40k per critical finding at preview pricing, BEFORE triage (The Information / Aaron Holmes, 2026-06-01; house arithmetic). Remediation cost: 'about $10' on a frontier model vs '$0.03 with the same results' on CRWD's Nemotron-based harness (Kurtz, GS Communacopia, 2026-09-10). Runtime products: 'fractions of a penny per transaction with near-zero latency' (MS, 2026-04-20).
ai-vuln-discovery-unit-cost.scope_note: Per-token price ≠ cost per FINDING ≠ cost per REMEDIATION ≠ cost per runtime TRANSACTION. The PANW figure is discovery only — 1,200 findings on its first test needed '3-4 months of cleaning to understand which ones are real' before returning to steady state (Arora, 2026-09-10) — so triage labour is outside the $1m. The CRWD $0.03 is a single-source management claim with no third-party verification. Mythos pricing is PREVIEW pricing for a gated model; expect it to fall.

variants.value: >24 criticals in ~3 weeks, ~5x normal tools, >$1m of tokens
variants.source: The Information / Aaron Holmes (Sam Rubin, SVP Unit 42)

variants.value: $10 (frontier) vs $0.03 (Nemotron harness) per remediation, 'same results'
1,200 vulnerabilities on PANW's first Mythos test → 3-4 months triage → steady state; find-mix 60% Mythos / 30% OpenAI / 10% other

ai-vuln-discovery-unit-cost.debate: If harness + multi-model stays 100-300x cheaper per unit of security work than a frontier model, capability gains TRANSFER to incumbents (the bull). If Mythos-class pricing falls ~10x while capability holds, the preventative layer (TENB/QLYS/RPD, pen-test services) is the first casualty and the harness advantage becomes a dependency. Watch: any packaged Anthropic security SKU with SOC-grade latency.
